data: Marble plaque, surviving in two joining fragments, missing the upper edge and right side, intact on left and below.
Text fills the face toeh stone, becoming cramped and slightly off horizontal towards the end.
Found prior to 1931 in building work on via Androne, in a tomb consisting of a narrow walled burial plot. The piece appears to have been lost already by the 1950s.

Apparatus criticus

  • Text of Agnello;
  • line.1: ἐντάδε sic AE 1933.25
  • line.8: ΛΥΓΗΣ sic AE 1933.25

English translation

Marta Fogagnolo

Here lies the blessed Apra, daughter of Kentianos and Asklepiodote, a good servant of Christ, a tree well planted in the faith, torn away from her brief life and from the affections of this world, leaving sorrow to her own. She returned the loan of her soul, dying on the Kalends of April during the fifteenth consulship of Theodosius and the fourth consulship of Valentinian.

Italian translation

Qui giace la beata Apra, figlia di Quinziano e di Asclepiodote, bouna serva di Cristo, albero ben piantato nella fede, dipartitasi dalla vita terrena e dagli affetti del mondo, lasciando dolore tra i suoi. Restitui il prestito della vita morendo il 1 aprile sotto il quindicesimo consolato di Teodosio ed il quarto di Valentiniano [trad. di Agnello]

commentary

The epitaph commemorates the young deceased Apra, daughter of Kentianos and Asklepiodote. For the name Apra, which may represent a variant of Apronia or Aphronia. The father's name is partially restored by Libertini (1931, 40), who also proposed alternative readings, including Sentianus, Gentianus, Ventianus, and Mintianus. The deceased is described as δούλη Χ(ριστο)ῦ ἀγαθή (ll. 3–4; cf. IG XIV 442 = ISic001267) and, through a poetic image, as δένδρο[ν καλῶς] | ἐν πίστει ἐφυτευμ[ένον (ll. 4–5), an expression that echoes a well-established image in Christian theology (cf. [Athan.] 28.712.45). The brevity of her life is conveyed by the expression τῇ ὀλιγοχρονίᾳ (l. 6) and by the reference to τοῖς ἰδίοις (l. 9), from whose affection she was torn away. The mention of her parents, together with the absence of any reference to a husband, led Libertini (1931, 41) to suggest that she died a virgin. At l. 10, the expression τῆς ψυχῆς δάνος refers to the soul as a loan that is returned to God after death. Finally, ll. 10–13 conclude the epitaph with the date of the deceased's death, which occurred on the Kalends of April during the fifteenth consulship of Theodosius and the fourth consulship of Valentinian. This internal dating places the inscription in AD 435.
